query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-Nb/Ta and non-titanium-rich single-phase HEA, enhancing local chemical short-range order through a minor elemental substitution will increase the electron–phonon coupling strength, thereby elevating the superconducting transition temperature (Tc).
generation.material_initial_state: A fully disordered, single-phase high-entropy alloy composed of at least five elements (each ≥5 atomic percent) that does not belong to the well‐studied Nb–Ta or titanium-rich families.
generation.intervention: Introduce a precise minor substitution designed to promote local chemical short-range order without causing phase separation, while maintaining overall composition and disorder at larger length scales.
generation.conditions: Synthesis must preserve the single-phase solid solution state (all elements ≥5 atomic percent) and measurements should be carried out under cryogenic conditions near the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical short-range order (atomic-scale variations in bonding environments) that emerges due to the controlled substitution.
generation.mechanism: The modified local atomic environments alter the electron–phonon coupling landscape by creating regions of enhanced coupling. This enhanced coupling facilitates stronger Cooper pairing, which in turn raises Tc compared to a baseline composition with maximal chemical randomness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy variant with increased local order will exhibit a measurable increase in Tc and corresponding changes in its phonon density of states (indicative of altered electron–phonon interactions) relative to the baseline disordered HEA.
generation.baseline: A similarly composed HEA synthesized to maximize random chemical distribution (minimal local order) used as the control sample.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected only when the solid solution state is maintained (i.e., no phase segregation) and within the low-temperature regime where superconductivity is observed. Outside these conditions, other factors may dominate superconducting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of Tc enhancement and the detailed quantitative change in electron–phonon coupling remain uncertain until experimental data is obtained.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA samples with identical overall composition. The control set is processed to maximize random atomic distribution, while the experimental set includes a targeted minor substitution to induce local short-range order. Characterize each sample’s local order using techniques such as atom probe tomography or high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, and then perform low-temperature measurements (e.g., resistivity vs temperature, specific heat, and spectroscopy) to determine Tc and probe phonon density of states.
measurements: Superconducting transition temperature (Tc) via resistivity or magnetic susceptibility measurements
Phonon density of states through spectroscopic methods
Local chemical ordering via atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental HEA with induced local order does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in Tc or detectable modifications in electron–phonon coupling (as inferred from the phonon density of states) relative to the baseline maximally disordered sample, then the hypothesis that local chemical short-range order enhances superconductivity is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The superconductivity of disordered materials has been extensively studied because of an observation made on the insulator-superconductor transition or disorder-induced superconductivity. In addition, recent studies on BiS2-based layered superconductors have shown the importance of controlling the local structural disorder to improve superconducting properties. As a new category of disordered superconductors, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are alloys containing five or more elements with an atomic concentration between 5 and 35%,, have been extensively studied, leading to the discovery of a wide range of HEA superconductors. One of the notable features is the difference in characteristics of superconductivity among conventional metal or alloy superconductors, superconducting thin films, and HEA superconductors,. Namely, the dependence of Tc on valence electron count (VEC) for HEAs exhibits interesting trends when that was compared with those for classical alloys (metals) and amorphous alloys. In the CsCl-type HEAs, the Tc-VEC exhibits opposite trend to that for the classical and amorphous alloys. In the α-Mn phase, although the trend of the Tc-VEC exhibits commonality among HEAs

It has long been recognized that a critical amount of disorder can suppress superconductivity near the Anderson quantum phase transition. The observed Tc reduction concomitant with a mixing entropy ΔS enhancement in superconducting HEAs seems to agree with that picture. On the other hand, recent analyses of competing interaction-channels in strongly disordered metals predict a Tc enhancement within the BCS framework, when the electron system is tuned to a quantum critical point,. This hypothesis finds support in a recent study of HEA (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x thin films; while each of the binary alloys TaNb and HfZrTi does not show a superconducting transition at or above 2 K, all solid solutions of (TaNb)1-x(HfZrTi)x at various mixing ratios x are superconducting at Tc≤6.9 K. This ’cocktail’ effect suggests an intricate relation between the presence of strong compositional disorder, realized through the random arrangement of five atomic species on a bcc lattice, and superconductivity, which is an interesting question to address experimentally.

frame.system: An uncharacterized high-entropy alloy that is a single-phase solid solution with at least five elements (each ≥5 atomic percent), not limited to well‐studied Nb–Ta or titanium-rich heavy transition metal systems.
frame.goal: To understand and control the superconducting behavior in these high-entropy alloys by identifying the key mechanistic drivers that set the superconducting transition temperature and pairing mechanism.
frame.limitation: Existing reports (primarily based on Nb–Ta matrices and titanium-rich systems) do not clearly establish which parameters govern superconductivity in the broader, compositional space of high-entropy alloys.

Investigations of titanium-rich systems that involve heavy transition metals and partial ordering, which provide insights into superconductivity but cannot be generalized to fully disordered, multi-element systems.
frame.understanding: A testable mechanistic hypothesis is that local chemical short-range order in the high-entropy alloy modulates the electron-phonon coupling strength. This modulation—stemming from fluctuations in atomic-scale bonding environments—directly influences the superconducting pairing mechanism and hence the critical temperature (Tc). The controlled comparison would involve synthesizing a baseline alloy with maximized chemical disorder and a variant where minor adjustments (e.g., substituting one element to favor slight local ordering without losing the single-phase constraint) are introduced. The prediction is that the variant will exhibit measurable differences in Tc and electron-phonon coupling constants (as evidenced by phonon density of states changes) relative to the baseline. Applicable boundary conditions include maintaining the solid solution state, keeping elemental concentrations above 5 atomic percent, and operating at cryogenic temperatures. Previously, evidence from Nb–Ta and titanium-rich high-entropy alloy systems suggests that lattice dynamics and disorder significantly affect superconducting parameters; however, these systems did not isolate the role of local chemical heterogeneities. An outcome that would falsify the hypothesis would be if the controlled adjustment in chemical short-range order produced no measurable change in Tc or electron-phonon coupling compared to the maximally disordered baseline, indicating that factors other than local order govern superconductivity in these alloys.

decision.trend: Early studies on superconducting high‐entropy alloys focused on demonstrating robust superconductivity in multi‐component systems (e.g., the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti HEA at ambient and high pressure, and later the inclusion of f‐elements in actinide‐bearing HEAs). These works established that superconductivity can persist in these disordered, multi‐element alloys, but they probed mainly the existence of superconductivity and its robustness under extreme conditions rather than the underlying mechanistic drivers. In particular, none of these earlier papers addressed how variations in local chemical environments, such as short‐range order, might modulate the electron–phonon coupling that governs the superconducting transition temperature.
decision.unsolved: The role of local chemical short‐range order in modulating electron–phonon coupling and hence superconductivity in disordered, multi‐element HEAs outside of the well‐studied Nb–Ta and titanium-rich systems remains unexplored. There is a lack of controlled comparisons that isolate how slight modifications in atomic-scale ordering, while preserving the single-phase solid solution constraint, can affect the superconducting pairing mechanism and Tc.
decision.lever: Introduce a precise alloy variant via a minor substitution that promotes local chemical short-range order without inducing phase separation, then perform low-temperature measurements (e.g., phonon density of states and Tc) to compare with a baseline maximally disordered HEA.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of demonstrating superconducting robustness while addressing the identified knowledge gap by isolating the effect of local chemical order. By controlling the level of short-range order through a targeted compositional tweak, researchers can directly test the hypothesis that enhanced local ordering modulates electron–phonon coupling, thereby causing measurable shifts in Tc relative to the baseline composition.
